title: Neem & tea tree shampoo bar
subtitle: A scalp-focused solid shampoo for oily or flaky conditions
excerpt: Cold-process shampoo bar with 10% neem oil and tea tree essential oil, formulated for oily or flaky scalp conditions. Made on a coconut, castor, and olive base with a low 3% superfat to avoid greasy residue. Yields six bars; hardens in 4-6 weeks.
sourceNotes: Susan Miller Cavitch, The Soapmaker's Companion (1997), shampoo bar formulation guidance; low superfat rates and coconut/castor ratios for hair. Soap-Calc SAP values (accessed 2026): coconut 0.190, castor 0.128, olive 0.134, neem 0.136. Tea tree EO in CP soap: stable at trace; 2% of oil weight is effective without irritation risk. Neem oil: strong odour; masks partially with tea tree but retain characteristic earthy note in finished bar.

recipe.batchNotes: Neem oil has a very strong garlic-like smell in its raw state; the tea tree partially masks this in the finished bar. Shampoo bars need a low superfat to avoid weighing hair down, keep the superfat at 3% or below for this formula.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Shampoo bars improve with a longer cure. At 6 weeks the bar is firm and lathers well; at 8 weeks it's better still.
recipe.shelfLifeNotes: 18 months in a cool, dry place. Neem oil oxidises faster than most soap fats; check the bar for rancid smell every few months if keeping a large batch. In use, keep the bar on a draining dish to extend its life.

glossaryTerms.definition: The chemical reaction between fat and lye (sodium hydroxide) that produces soap. All oils in this formula, including the neem, contribute to the saponification and are included in the total oil weight for lye calculation.
The percentage of oil left unsaponified in the finished bar. Shampoo bars use a lower superfat than body soap (3% rather than 5-7%) to avoid a greasy residue on hair.
The point at which the soap batter thickens enough to hold a faint drizzled trail, the signal to add essential oils and pour into the mould.

content.text: Neem and tea tree shampoo bar is a solid cold-process shampoo formulated for oily or flaky scalp conditions. Neem oil at 10% of the oil weight brings a reputation for scalp care developed over centuries of Ayurvedic use; tea tree essential oil adds a clean, medicinal note and helps moderate the strong earthy smell of raw neem. The bar is built on a coconut-dominant base for lather, with castor oil for slip and olive for mild conditioning. A 3% superfat keeps it from leaving residue on hair. Six bars; hardens in 4-6 weeks.

content.text: Put on protective gloves and goggles. Work in a ventilated space. Pour the sodium hydroxide slowly into the distilled water in the HDPE pitcher, stirring until dissolved. Cool to 38-42°C.
Melt the coconut oil, then combine with the neem oil, olive oil, and castor oil. The neem oil has a distinctive earthy, garlic-like smell that is normal. Bring to 38-42°C.

Pour into the mould, insulate, and leave 24-48 hours. Unmould when firm. Cut into 6 bars wearing gloves.

Wet hair and the bar thoroughly. Rub the bar between the palms to build a lather, then work through the scalp with fingertips. Rinse thoroughly, soap-based shampoo bars need a good rinse to remove all residue. Some people find a diluted apple cider vinegar rinse (1 tablespoon per cup of water, applied after shampooing and rinsed off) helps during the adjustment period when switching from detergent shampoo.
Keep the bar on a draining soap dish, a wet shampoo bar left sitting in water dissolves quickly. Store extra bars in a cool, dry place. The

is kept low on purpose; the bar cleans well without conditioning residue. Shelf life is 18 months; the neem component oxidises faster than most soap fats. Discard if the bar develops a clearly rancid smell or orange spots.
